# Progression patterns and clinical outcomes in patients with cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma following anti-PD-1 therapy failure

**Authors:** K Khaddour; P Kote; M Liu; A Giobbie-Hurder; I Dryg; A Goyal; JP Guenette; JD Schoenfeld; DN Margalit; RB Tishler; EM Rettig; RKV Sethi; DJ Annino; LA Goguen; R Uppaluri; C Yoon; M de Simone; NA Ran; J Stevens; AH Waldman; ES Ruiz; JV Cohen; AW Silk; GJ Hanna

**Affiliations:** 1Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, USA

## Abstract

Anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy is the cornerstone for managing advanced cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma (CSCC). Nevertheless, many patients experience treatment failure. Limited data exist regarding outcomes following anti-PD-1 failure. This study investigates progression patterns and clinical outcomes in CSCC patients post-anti-PD-1 therapy.

We conducted a retrospective analysis of CSCC patients treated with anti-PD-1 at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. We evaluated clinicopathological features and outcomes. Overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. CSCC-specific mortality was estimated using cumulative incidence. Multivariate regression was used to investigate prognostic factors.

Among 238 patients receiving immunotherapy, 72 exhibited anti-PD-1 failure with a median age of 72 years; 22% were female and 29% were immunosuppressed. Median follow-up was 23 months [95% confidence interval (CI) 19-37 months] and median duration of immunotherapy was 3 months (range 1-44 months). Progression after anti-PD-1 failure occurred as local (21%), locoregional (37%), or distant metastatic (42%). Primary resistance was observed in 62.5%, while 37.5% developed secondary resistance. Patients with primary resistance exhibited a significantly lower tumor mutational burden (TMB) (P = 0.03). Among 61 patients receiving subsequent treatment, cetuximab-based therapy and local treatments each were administered in 31%. Complete and partial responses were achieved in 5% and 25%, respectively, while 6% had stable disease, 28% progressed, and 36% were non-assessable. Median OS was 44.1 months (95% CI 17.4 months-not achieved) and median EFS2 (time from starting subsequent treatment post-anti-PD-1 until recurrence, progression, or death) was 7.1 months (95% CI 3.2-12.2 months). CSCC-specific death was 50% at 5 years (95% CI 30% to 67%). Prior chemotherapy was associated with poorer OS (hazard ratio 2.87, 95% CI 1.03-7.98, P = 0.04).

In this cohort of patients with CSCC, distant metastatic and locoregional progression were the predominant patterns following anti-PD-1 failure, with lower TMB linked to primary resistance. Prior chemotherapy was associated with poorer OS. Select patients benefited from subsequent treatments, including cetuximab and local therapy.

Key words: cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, anti-PD-1, cemiplimab, immunotherapy, resistance, outcomes

## Abstract

This study characterizes patterns of cutaneous squamous cell cancer progression after anti-PD-1 therapy.

Clinical and molecular correlations of primary versus secondary resistance are identified.

Outcomes of subsequent treatments and factors linked to survival are evaluated.

## Introduction

Cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma (CSCC) is the second most prevalent cancer worldwide, with most cases initially presenting as localized disease. This early-stage CSCC is typically managed effectively through surgical intervention alone, with adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) and recently anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy being utilized in high-risk cases, resulting in favorable outcomes.1 However, ∼5% of patients present with advanced CSCC at the time of diagnosis, characterized by unresectable or recurrent tumors, regional lymph node involvement, or distant metastases.2,3

The advent of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has revolutionized the therapeutic landscape for skin cancer, including CSCC. Cemiplimab, an anti-PD-1 therapy, was the first systemic immunotherapy approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for CSCC, based on high objective response rates and prolonged duration of response (DOR) in the EMPOWER study.4 The long-term follow-up from cemiplimab trials in advanced CSCC demonstrated a response rate of 46.4%, a progression-free survival (PFS) of 21.7 months, and a median overall survival (OS) of 48.4 months.5 Other anti-PD-1 therapies including pembrolizumab have shown comparable efficacy in patients with locally advanced, recurrent or metastatic CSCC in the KEYNOTE-629 study,6,7 and recently an anti-programmed death-ligand 1 drug was approved by the FDA for advanced CSCC.8

Despite advances in the management of CSCC, cancer progression during or after anti-PD-1 therapy remains a challenge, with a progression rate of 23.3% in the KEYNOTE-629 study6 and 14% in the EMPOWER study. The 12-month PFS rate was ∼45% in KEYNOTE-629, while the estimated event-free probability for DOR at 12 months was 81% in EMPOWER.5 Collectively, these trials highlight a subset of patients who either do not respond to anti-PD-1 or later develop resistance after initial response. The mechanisms driving failure to anti-PD-1 therapy remain poorly understood, and subsequent treatments, including chemotherapy, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors like cetuximab, and local interventions (surgery and/or RT), are not well studied.9 Furthermore, there is a paucity of clinical trials addressing optimal treatment approaches for patients with CSCC who experience treatment failure with anti-PD-1 therapy.

This study examines progression patterns and clinical outcomes in patients with CSCC following anti-PD-1 therapy failure, with the goal of informing future clinical trials and management strategies.

## Patients and methods

### Study cohort

We conducted a retrospective analysis using electronic health records from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, MA) to identify patients diagnosed with CSCC who received ICIs (including patients receiving treatment in the neoadjuvant and palliative settings), specifically PD-1 inhibitors such as cemiplimab, pembrolizumab, and nivolumab. Patients treated with a combination of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 inhibitor (ipilimumab) and anti-PD-1 therapy were also included. Patients who received immunotherapy and did not experience recurrence or progression, and those who did not have sufficient follow-up data (did not receive their post-ICI treatment at our institution) were excluded from analysis. The study was approved by the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center (DF/HCC) Institutional Review Board (protocol #22-088) and included patients treated at the Centers for Cutaneous Oncology and Head and Neck Cancer between April 2016 and January 2025. The cohort comprised patients who experienced disease progression during or after treatment with anti-PD-1. Data collected included demographics, clinicopathological features (e.g. tumor location, genomic profiling), initial treatment before immunotherapy, tumor stage at anti-PD-1 initiation, and history of immunosuppression. Immunosuppression was defined as a history of human immunodeficiency virus infection, concomitant hematologic malignancies, solid organ transplant, or autoimmune disorders requiring systemic immunosuppressive medication. Subsequent treatments post-anti-PD-1 and clinical outcomes were documented.

### Genomic sequencing

Patients consented to genomic testing as part of clinical care or research protocols. Molecular testing was conducted by a Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)-certified laboratory. Eligibility required tumor samples with >20% tumor content on hematoxylin–eosin slide review. Sequencing depth ranged from 80× to 640×, with a minimum of 50× required for quality control. Given no established threshold for high versus low tumor mutational burden (TMB) in CSCC, we used the definition of high TMB as ≥10 mutations/megabase according to KEYNOTE-158, which established the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy in tumors with high TMB. Nineteen genes were selected for reporting based on the literature on driver mutations in CSCC.10,11 UV signature was considered positive if the tumor exhibited an elevated mutational burden, including an increased number of C>T transitions, enriched at dipyrimidine (CC, CT, TC) sites, which is characteristic of UV light-induced DNA damage.12

### Efficacy and outcome endpoints

The best overall response (BOR) to systemic therapy, including anti-PD-1 and subsequent treatments, was confirmed via radiological reports and treating investigator assessments. For clinical evaluation to assess BOR, digital medical photography was used when feasible. BOR for the first subsequent treatment post-anti-PD-1 was also recorded. Patients receiving local treatment (surgery and/or RT) were considered non-assessable. Progression was considered local if it occurred at the site of the primary CSCC lesion without the presence of in-transit metastases or lymph node involvement. Locoregional disease was defined as involvement of regional lymph nodes or in-transit metastases, and distant metastatic disease was defined as having distant metastases.

Resistance to anti-PD-1 was defined as primary (progression within 6 months of therapy initiation) or secondary (progression after 6 months), which is also referred to as acquired resistance.

OS was defined as the time from initiation of anti-PD-1 to death from any cause or last follow-up. Event-free survival (EFS) was used instead of PFS as some patients were treated with anti-PD-1 in the neoadjuvant setting and experienced disease recurrence rather than disease progression. EFS1 was defined as the time from anti-PD-1 initiation to either disease progression, recurrence, or death, whichever occurred first; patients without an event were censored at the time of last follow-up. EFS2 was defined as the time from the start of the subsequent treatment that was administered to patients after anti-PD-1 until subsequent disease progression, recurrence, or death.

### Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient characteristics. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were reported as medians with ranges, unless otherwise specified.

OS, EFS1, and EFS2 were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with median survival times and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated using log transformations. Competing risk analyses for CSCC-specific death were carried out using a sub-distribution hazard model, accounting for the competing risk of non-CSCC death. Non-parametric cumulative incidence estimates of CSCC-specific death were reported at 1, 3, and 5 years. The cumulative incidence of progression patterns, including local, locoregional, and metastatic progression during or after the use of anti-PD-1 therapy, was empirically estimated since all patients had an event.

Univariate analyses examined the associations between clinical variables (e.g. immunosuppression status, tumor location, prior therapies) and OS. Associations were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models with hazard ratios (HRs), CIs, and P values reported. Variables with P < 0.05 in univariate analysis were included in multivariate models. Statistical analyses were carried out in R (version 4.3.2, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Oncoplots were generated using the comut Python package.13 Mann–Whitney U tests compared TMB between the primary and secondary resistance groups, and Fisher’s exact tests assessed gene enrichment differences in these groups.

## Results

Between April 2016 and January 2025, a total of 238 patients with CSCC received anti-PD-1-based immunotherapy. Among these, 72 patients (30%) experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after treatment with immunotherapy (Supplementary Figure S1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.106081). The cohort’s characteristics are described in Table 1, with a median follow-up duration (time since starting anti-PD-1) of 23.4 months (95% CI 19.6-37.4 months). The cohort included 16 females (22%) and 21 immunocompromised individuals (29%). At initial diagnosis, the primary tumor location was the head and neck in 40 patients (55.6%), trunk and extremities in 26 (36.1%), and unknown in 6 (8.3%). Before anti-PD-1 therapy, 53 patients (73.6%) received local or systemic therapy, including surgery (41.7%), surgery with RT or chemo-RT (25%), and chemotherapy with RT (6.9%). According to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) eighth edition staging at anti-PD-1 initiation, 2 patients (2.8%) were stage II, 39 (54.2%) stage III, and 31 (43.1%) stage IV. Cemiplimab was the most frequently administered anti-PD-1 therapy in 55 patients (76.4%).

### Treatment outcomes on anti-PD-1 therapy

The BOR to anti-PD-1 therapy was complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) in 29 patients (40.3%), while 43 patients (59.7%) exhibited stable disease (SD) or progressive disease (PD). The median anti-PD-1 treatment duration was 3 months (range 1-44 months). Among those with disease progression and recurrence, 45 patients (62.5%) had primary resistance and 27 (37.5%) developed secondary resistance. Anti-PD-1 therapy was discontinued in 11 patients (15.3%) due to unacceptable toxicity, and 22 patients (30.6%) were rechallenged with anti-PD-1. The most common progression pattern was distant metastatic disease in 30 patients (42%), followed by locoregional in 27 patients (37%) and local progression in 15 patients (21%) (Figure 1A). The cumulative incidence of progression was highest in patients with locoregional disease and those with distant metastases (Figure 1B). At progression, distant metastatic sites included skin/subcutaneous in 15 patients (50%), lymph nodes in 17 (56.7%), lung in 12 (40%), bone in 10 (33.3%), liver in 4 (13%), and soft tissue in 4 (13%) (Figure 1C).

*Figure 1: Metastatic site transitions and progression dynamics after anti-PD-1 failure in patients with CSCC. (A) Sankey diagram of the metastatic site transition at three different timepoints (n = 72). (B) Cumulative incidence of progression patterns after failure to anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy (n = 72). (C) Sites of distant metastases at the time of progression to anti-PD-1 therapy.*

Genomic sequencing data were available for 20 patients (27.7%), with genomic and clinical characteristics depicted in Figure 2. The most prevalent mutations were TP53 (90%), CDKN2A (85%), NOTCH1 (70%), KMT2D (65%), and FAT1 (60%). The median TMB was 39.69 (range 3-114). Among these 20 patients, 14 (70%) developed primary resistance, and 6 (30%) developed secondary resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy. A positive UV signature was detected in 13 patients (65%) and negative in 3 (15%), and not evaluable in 4 (20%). Median TMB was significantly lower in patients with primary resistance compared with those with secondary resistance (23.19 versus 71.51, P = 0.03; Supplementary Figure S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.106081). No significant differences in mutation enrichment were observed between primary and secondary resistance, although TP53 showed a trend toward primary resistance (P = 0.08), and HRAS trended toward secondary resistance (P = 0.06).

*Figure 2: Genomic landscape and clinical characteristics of a subgroup of patients who developed resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy. CR, complete response; PD, progressive disease; PR, partial response; SD, stable disease; TMB, tumor mutational burden.*

Seven patients received neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy. All developed either clinical or pathological progression before or at the time of surgery. Six patients subsequently underwent surgery with curative intent; one patient did not proceed to resection because of in-transit metastases that were not amenable to surgery. All seven patients experienced local or locoregional, but not distant, recurrence and were treated with adjuvant radiotherapy, with or without a radiosensitizing agent. No further disease recurrence was observed in any patient during their reported follow-up period.

### Clinical outcomes on subsequent treatment after failure to anti-PD-1 therapy

Median OS for the study cohort was 44.1 months (95% CI 17.4 months-not achieved; Figure 3A). Median EFS1 was 3.4 months (95% CI 2.8-6.1 months; Figure 3B). At progression, 61 patients (84.7%) received subsequent treatment. The median EFS2 was 7.1 months (95% CI 3.2-12.2 months; Figure 3C). There were 29 deaths in the cohort, with 23 attributed to CSCC. The cumulative incidence of CSCC-specific death was 17% at 1 year, 33% at 3 years, and 50% at 5 years (Figure 3D). The treatment timeline for anti-PD-1 and subsequent treatments is illustrated in Figure 4A. The median number of treatment regimens post-anti-PD-1 was 1 (range 1-11). Subsequent treatments included cetuximab-based therapies in 19 patients (31.1%), local therapy (surgery and/or RT) in 19 (31.1%), immunotherapy in 13 (21.3%), chemotherapy in 6 (9.8%), and clinical trials in 4 (6.6%) (Figure 4B). The best response in assessable patients to the subsequent treatment was CR in 3 patients (5%), PR in 15 (25%), SD in 4 (6%), and PD in 17 (28%), while 36% were non-assessable.

In univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses, we explored the prognostic value of several factors on OS including: (i) therapy (systemic treatment and RT) administered to treat CSCC before anti-PD-1 therapy, (ii) immunosuppression status, and (iii) tumor location on the head and neck (Supplementary Figure S3, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.106081). Only prior systemic chemotherapy was significantly associated with increased mortality risk (HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.03-7.98, P = 0.04). These parameters did not significantly impact BOR to anti-PD-1 therapy (Supplementary Figure S4, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.106081).

Of the 22 patients rechallenged with anti-PD-1 therapy (30.5%), 17 (77%) were assessable. Seven patients (41%) responded to the rechallenge, of which four were patients who had disease remission for at least 1 year after stopping anti-PD-1 therapy and before progression and rechallenge.

## Discussion

This study provides a comprehensive analysis of progression patterns and clinical outcomes in patients with CSCC following anti-PD-1 therapy failure. In our cohort, 30% of patients experienced disease progression after anti-PD-1 therapy, a rate comparable to that reported in prior trials of cemiplimab in advanced CSCC.14 Notably, primary resistance, defined as disease progression within 6 months of initiating anti-PD-1 therapy, emerged as the predominant manifestation of treatment failure.

The progression patterns observed in our cohort, predominantly locoregional and metastatic, are consistent with established literature, with lymph nodes, cutaneous/subcutaneous tissue, and lungs being the most common sites of metastases. Genomic sequencing data, albeit limited, suggested a lower TMB in patients with primary resistance compared with those with secondary resistance. While no significant difference in genomic alterations was identified between resistance groups, the small sample size necessitates cautious interpretation. Previous studies have implicated specific chromosomal gains and gene enrichment in response to anti-PD-1 therapy, warranting further investigation in larger cohorts.11,15

A significant portion of patients (15%) did not pursue subsequent treatment post-anti-PD-1 therapy, opting for best supportive care, reflecting advanced disease and poor performance status. The median EFS2 (in 61 patients receiving subsequent treatment) was 7 months, highlighting the limited efficacy of current therapeutic options beyond anti-PD-1. The predominance of single-line subsequent treatments received by 50% of patients further emphasizes the challenges in managing CSCC post-immunotherapy failure.

Salvage local therapies and cetuximab-containing regimens were common post-anti-PD-1 interventions in our cohort, with a response rate of 30% among assessable patients. These findings are consistent with existing literature, suggesting that cetuximab may offer a viable option for select patients with disease progression post-anti-PD-1.9,16 Recent reports and trials, such as the I-TACKLE study, have explored the potential of combining cetuximab with anti-PD-1 therapy to increase response rates, suggesting synergism between PD-1 and EGFR inhibition in CSCC.17, 18, 19

Our analysis also highlights the prognostic implications of prior systemic treatment before anti-PD-1 therapy, demonstrating a significant association with increased mortality risk. Perhaps, this suggests that anti-PD-1 therapy should be prioritized in the treatment algorithm for CSCC, particularly given the emerging evidence supporting its use in the neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. Alternatively, the results may indicate a more aggressive disease biology in those patients requiring prior systemic chemotherapy.

Interestingly, our study observed higher response rates in patients rechallenged with anti-PD-1 therapy compared with previous pooled analyses, suggesting potential benefits in select patient populations including those who discontinue treatment and experience durable response beyond 1 year before progression. The retrospective nature and single-center design of this study imposes limitations, necessitating validation in larger, multicenter cohorts. In addition, we could not evaluate and compare different subsequent therapies given the small number of patients and variation in subsequent treatment. Collectively, this study underscores the complexity of managing CSCC post-anti-PD-1 therapy failure, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies and personalized approaches to improve outcomes. Future research should focus on elucidating the mechanisms of resistance and exploring novel therapeutic approaches to enhance the efficacy of existing treatments.

### Conclusion

In this cohort of patients with CSCC including patients who received anti-PD-1 therapy in the neoadjuvant and palliative settings, the most common pattern of progression during or after anti-PD-1 therapy failure was distant metastatic disease. Lower TMB was significantly associated with primary resistance. Administration of systemic chemotherapy before treatment with anti-PD-1 was associated with worse OS. Subsequent treatments including cetuximab, local therapy, or rechallenge with anti-PD-1 yielded responses in a subset of patients. Larger studies are warranted to investigate treatment strategies after anti-PD-1 progression.
